description: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
summary:
AnalogExplorer is an open web app that finds where on Earth to rehearse missions to permanent Moon base sites and Mars sites, and says plainly what Earth cannot reproduce. It compares all 23,039 land tiles of the Earth (1° × 1°)
with seven targets: the Shackleton and Malapert regions at the lunar south pole, the Mare Tranquillitatis pit, and Jezero, Gale, Arcadia Planitia and Oxia Planum on Mars. The comparison covers 10 variables in 5 dimensions (topography, temperature, water and ice, illumination, surface cover), computed with the same physics from NASA, ESA and CNES open data. For a chosen mission (rover, solar panels, drilling, habitat), the app ranks distinct sites, shows variable by variable where each analogy holds or breaks, finds the 2–3 sites that together cover a
target best, highlights under-studied places, measures the robustness of every result, and reports the conditions no place on Earth reaches. A credibility check fixed in advance tests the method against known analogs, and its results are shown as they are.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

No single place on Earth reproduces the Moon or Mars, and space agencies choose their analogs by function: a site is good for one property, not all of them. AnalogExplorer is built on that idea: characterize before ranking.

- Data. Every land tile of the Earth (1° × 1°, about 110 km) and a window of the same size around each of the seven targets are described by the distribution (19 quantiles) of 10 variables: slope and roughness; diurnal temperature amplitude and minimum temperature; aridity and ground below 0 °C at depth; mean insolation, sunlit fraction and Sun elevation; bare ground. Each variable is defined physically and computed with the same operator on the three worlds, at a common topographic scale of about 463 m, from NASA POWER, LRO LOLA and Diviner, MGS MOLA, NASA PGDA, the Copernicus DEM, ESA WorldCover, the SCAR Antarctic Digital Database and the Mars Climate Database.

- Similarity. The gap between a site and a target is the Wasserstein distance between distributions, read in units of the typical gap between two random places on Earth's land. A variable that no place on Earth can match (beyond 99 % of Earth–Earth gaps, such as the lunar day–night amplitude) leaves the score and goes to the limits report, instead of dictating the ranking.

- Score. Mission profiles (rover mobility, solar panels, drilling and resource use, habitat and construction) weight the five dimensions; an expert mode sets the weights by hand. The score is a weighted geometric mean, so a strong variable never hides a weak one. Non-maximum suppression keeps distinct sites at least 300 km apart.

- Beyond the rank. A novelty axis highlights under-studied sites far from the 29 catalogued analogs; 300 Monte-Carlo draws on the weights measure robustness; a search over all combinations of candidate sites (greedy for very large pools) finds the 2–3 sites that together cover a target best; an 11 km zoom locates the best terrain inside each site; a "When to go" calendar gives the months when the Sun stands most like on the target.

- Honesty. Every site comes with a profile by dimension, the conditions Earth cannot reproduce (gravity, vacuum, radiation, and out-of-range variables with figures), and a downloadable site sheet. A credibility check, fixed before looking at the results, asks whether known analogs rank better than random places on the properties they are famous for: it passes for the four Martian targets (p < 0.001, still after a Holm correction) and fails for the three lunar targets, which the app states as is.

- App. Six pages: home, target and mission, multi-dimensional profile, complementary ensemble, limits report and site sheet, and an Earth atlas that answers the reverse question: which world does a given place resemble?

Example (Jezero crater, habitat mission): the best distinct site is the Kunlun Mountains in China, 712 km from the nearest catalogued analog. It matches the terrain, the dryness and the bare ground, but not the thermal cycle or the lighting. Two sites together, Enderby Land (Antarctica) and Balochistan (Iran), reproduce 0.89 of the target's weighted conditions, against 0.56 for the best single site.

What benefits does it have?

- It answers the practical question of a mission team: where to test what, and what such a test cannot tell.

- Every number is traceable to an open dataset, a formula and a fixed threshold; the written atlas and the site sheets are generated by rules from the data, never by a language model.

- It runs in a browser, without an account, on a computer or a phone; the code is open (MIT licence), tested (136 automated tests on every change) and reproducible (pinned versions, fixed random seeds).

What is the intended impact?

AnalogExplorer helps agencies, researchers and field teams choose complementary Earth test sites for Artemis and Mars missions, and look beyond the famous analog regions. It also makes the limits of terrestrial analogs explicit, so that rover, drilling, habitat or solar-array tests are planned where Earth is representative and not trusted where it is not. The method is open and general: new targets or variables can be added with the same pipeline.

What tools did you use?

Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, rasterio and GDAL for remote reading of cloud-optimized rasters), Streamlit and Plotly for the web app, pytest and ruff for tests and code quality, GitHub Actions for continuous integration on Python 3.12 and 3.15, and Streamlit Community Cloud for hosting. Open data was read from the AWS Registry of Open Data (NASA POWER, Copernicus DEM, ESA WorldCover), the NASA PDS Geosciences Node, NASA PGDA and the Mars Climate Database web service.

How is the project creative?

- It characterizes before it ranks: the main output is a profile by dimension, not a single score.

- It treats analogs as a team, our answer to the challenge's "Surprise us": instead of one winner, a complementary set of 2–3 sites covers each other's gaps, and covers a target better than any single place (Jezero: 0.89 with two sites, 0.56 with the best one).

- It reports what Earth cannot do as a result in its own right, with figures, instead of hiding it in a score.

- It answers the reverse question, from any place on Earth to the world it resembles most.

- It tests itself: a credibility check fixed in advance, whose negative results are published.

What factors did your team consider?

- Scale: tiles of about 110 km for a global screening, then an 11 km terrain zoom inside each site; climate stays at the scale of its 0.5° to 1° grids, which the app states.

- Comparability: the same physical definition and operator on three worlds; values fixed by physics (no liquid water or vegetation on the Moon and Mars) are written and sourced in the code.

- Bias: every share of the Earth is a share of land area, so the many narrow polar tiles do not weigh more than their surface; famous analog regions are flagged so that under-studied places stand out.

- Uncertainty: mission weights are expert judgements, so robustness and a score range are shown for every site.

- Validity: a protocol fixed in advance, a correction for testing seven targets, and results reported as they are, including failures; the app never shows invented data.
